source_text: Sed et omni petenti me dabo in causa eleemesynae, non in coneussurae. Petenti inquit. Porro qui concutit, non petit. Qui comminatur, si non acceperit, non postulat, sed exterquet. Non eleemesynam expectat qui non miserandus, sed timendus vanit. Da(??)o igitur misericordiae, non timiditatis meae nomine, ubi qui accepit deum honorat et benedictionem mihi reddit, non ubi amplius et benefactum praestitisse se credit et praedam suam aspiciens dicit: De reatu. Irascar et in inimicum? Sed inimicitiae et alios habent titulos. Non tamen dixit traditorem aut persecutorem aut concussorem. Nam huic quanto magis carbones acervabo super caput, si me non redemero? Proinde, inquit, qui tibi tunicam sustulerit, vel etiam pallium concede. Ad eum pertinet, qui rem, non qui fidem meam eripere quaesierit. Concedam et pallium non minanti traditionem. Si minatus fuerit, etiam tunicam reposcam. Omnium iam nunc domini sententiarum suae sunt et causae et regulae. Termini non in infinitum nec ad omnia spectant. Atque adeo omni petenti dari iubet, ipse signum petentibus non dat. Alioquin si omnibus passim petentibus dandum putas, tu mihi videris, non dico vinum febricitanti, sed etiam venenum aut gladium mor(??)m desideranti daturus. Facite autem vobis amicos de mammona, quomodo intellegendum sit, parabola praemissa te doceat. Ad populum Iudaicum dictum, qui, commissam sibi rationem demini cum male administrasset, deberet de mammonae hominibus, quod nos eramus, amicos sibi potius prospicere quam inimicos, et relevare nos a debitis peccatorum, quibus deo detinebamur, si nobis id dominica ratione conferrent, ut, cum coepisset ab his deficere gratia, ad nostram fidem refugientes reciperentur in tabernacula aeterna. Quamvis nunc puta aliam interpretationem parabolae et sententiae istius, dum scias verisimile non esse, ut concussores nostri in amicitiam redacti per mammonam recipiant tunc nos in tabernacula aeterna. Sed quid non timiditas persuadebit? Quasi et fugere scriptum permittat et redimere praecipiat. Parum denique est, si unus aut alius ita eruitur. Massaliter totae ecclesiae tributum sibi irrogaverunt. Nescio dolendum an crubescendum sit, cum in matricibus beneficiariorum et curiosorum inter tabernarios et (??)ianeos et fures balnearum et aleones et lenones Christiani quoque vectigales continentur. Hanc episcopatui formam apostoli providentius condiderunt, ut regno suo securi frui possent, sub obtentu procurandi(??)? Scilicet enim talem pacem Christus ad patrem regrediens mandavit a militibus per Saturnalia redimendam!
thought_title: Giving, not extortion; mammon-friends and the shame of taxed churches
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that Christians may pay their way out of persecution, and he now distinguishes true almsgiving from paying extortionists, then turns to the parable of the unjust steward and the shame of churches paying tribute.
pass_a_gloss: But also to everyone asking me I will give in the cause of almsgiving, not in the cause of extortion. To the one asking, he says. Furthermore he who extorts does not ask. He who threatens, if he will not have received, does not request, but wrings out. He does not expect almsgiving who has come not to be pitied, but to be feared. Therefore I will give in the name of mercy, not of my cowardice, where he who has received honors God and returns a blessing to me, not where he believes he has rendered a service and looking at his booty says: About the guilt. Shall I be angry also at an enemy? But enmities also have other titles. Yet he did not say betrayer or persecutor or extortionist. For upon this one how much more will I heap coals upon his head, if I will not have bought my way out? Accordingly, he says, the one who will have taken your tunic, also give even your cloak. It pertains to him who has sought to take away my property, not my faith. I will give also my cloak to one not threatening betrayal. If he will have threatened, I will demand back even my tunic. Now all the Lord's sayings have their own causes and rules. Their boundaries do not extend into infinity nor do they look to all things. And so he commands to give to everyone asking, yet he himself does not give a sign to those asking. Otherwise if you think it must be given to all indiscriminately asking, you seem to me to be about to give, I do not say wine to one with fever, but even poison or a sword to one desiring death. But make for yourselves friends from money, how it must be understood, let the parable set before you teach you. It was said to the Jewish people, who, when they had badly administered the account of the master entrusted to them, ought to look out for friends for themselves from the men of money, which we were, rather than enemies, and to relieve us from the debts of sins, by which we were held to God, if they would confer this to us by the master's account, so that, when grace had begun to fail from them, fleeing to our faith they might be received into eternal tabernacles. Although now suppose another interpretation of the parable and of this saying, while you know it is not likely, that our extortionists, brought into friendship through money, would then receive us into eternal tabernacles. But what will cowardice not persuade? As if Scripture both permits flight and commands buying one's way out. Finally it is too little, if one or another is thus rescued. In masses whole churches have imposed tribute upon themselves. I do not know whether it must be grieved over or blushed over, when in the registers of beneficiaries and informers among tavern-keepers and bath-thieves and gamblers and pimps Christians also are contained as taxpayers. Did the apostles provide this form for the episcopate, so that they might enjoy their kingdom securely, under the pretext of administering? Surely Christ returning to the Father commanded such a peace to be bought from soldiers through the Saturnalia!

choices.why: The glossary does not ban this term, and it renders the Greek loanword eleemosyna in its ordinary sense of charitable giving, contrasting with extortion.
The glossary gives 'extortionist' for concussor; concussura is the abstract noun of the same root, so 'extortion' keeps the family connection.
The glossary requires 'cowardice' for timiditas, and this is the genitive of the same noun.
The glossary requires 'buying one's way out' for redemptio; the verb redimo here is the first-person future perfect of the same action, so 'buy my way out' preserves the glossary term.
The glossary requires 'money' for mammona, and this is the ablative governed by de.
The glossary requires 'extortionist' for concussor; the plural follows the same rendering.

pass_b_english: But I will give to everyone who asks me when the cause is almsgiving, not extortion. "To the one who asks," he says (Matthew 5:42). But the extortionist does not ask. The one who threatens, if he does not receive, does not request; he wrings it out. The man who comes not to be pitied but to be feared is not looking for almsgiving. So I will give in the name of mercy, not of my own cowardice, where the one who receives honors God and returns a blessing to me, not where he thinks he has done me an even greater favor and, looking at his booty, says, "Consider this your payment for guilt."

Will I be angry even at an enemy? But enmities have other grounds as well. Yet he did not say "the betrayer" or "the persecutor" or "the extortionist." For how much more will I heap coals on his head if I do not buy my way out (Romans 12:20)? "Therefore," he says, "if someone takes your tunic, give him your cloak as well" (Matthew 5:40). That applies to the one who tries to take my property, not my faith. I will give my cloak too, but not to the one threatening betrayal. If he threatens, I will demand my tunic back.

All the Lord's sayings now have their own occasions and rules. Their boundaries do not extend infinitely or apply to everything. And indeed he commands giving to everyone who asks, yet he himself does not give a sign to those who ask. Otherwise, if you think we must give to everyone who asks indiscriminately, you seem to me ready to give, I will not say wine to a feverish man, but even poison or a sword to one who desires death.

"Make friends for yourselves by means of money" (Luke 16:9). Let the parable that comes before it teach you how this should be understood. It was spoken to the Jewish people, who had badly administered the stewardship entrusted to them. They ought to provide for themselves friends rather than enemies from among the people of money, that is, from us, and they ought to relieve us of the debts of sins by which we were held bound to God, if they would grant us this according to the Lord's accounting. Then, when grace began to fail them, they might flee to our faith and be received into eternal dwellings.

For now, suppose some other interpretation of that parable and saying, as long as you know it is not likely that our extortionists, brought into friendship through money, will then receive us into eternal dwellings. But what will cowardice not persuade? As if Scripture permits flight and commands buying one's way out.

Finally, it is not enough if one or another is rescued in this way. Whole churches have imposed a tax on themselves en masse. I do not know whether to grieve or blush when Christians are listed as taxpayers in the registers of beneficiaries and informers, among tavern-keepers and doorkeepers and bathhouse thieves and gamblers and pimps. Did the apostles establish this pattern for the episcopate with such foresight, so that they could enjoy their rule in security under the pretext of administration? Surely this is the peace Christ commanded when he returned to the Father, to be bought from soldiers during the Saturnalia!

mor(??)m: the source has damage; the intended word is likely 'mortem' (death), and the gloss renders it as such.
procurandi(??): the source has damage; the intended word is likely 'procurandi' (of administering), and the gloss renders it as such.
(??)ianeos: the source has damage; the word is uncertain, possibly 'balneaneos' or similar, rendered as 'bath-thieves' in the gloss.
